name: Public Speaking
description: A half-credit course developing confident, effective oral communication skills for academic and professional contexts. Students study speech preparation, audience analysis, delivery techniques, and persuasive strategies through a series of progressively challenging speaking assignments.

modules.title: Overview of Public Speaking
modules.objectives: Identify the communication process model and its components; explain why public speaking competence matters in academic and professional contexts; describe the characteristics of an ethical public speaker.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §1.2 for communication models. The speaker encodes a message, the audience decodes it, and voice, gesture, or a digital medium provides channels. Feedback is an audience response; noise is interference; context includes occasion, setting, and cultural expectations. Communication can be simultaneous rather than a one-way transfer. Ethical speaking requires accurate claims, source acknowledgment, preparation, and respect for audience differences. In the supplied reuse-station speech, the student is the sender, the council the audience, and funding the requested response; a confused expression is feedback, while an unexplained technical term can be semantic noise.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Overview of Public Speaking. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Read §19.1 for audience, purpose, and public communication. Worked ethical distinction: twelve recycling bins and seven trash cans are counts of containers, not amounts of paper or proof of daily school-wide waste. Practice: name the missing observation needed to support the opening claim, identify a possible channel and noise source, and write one clarification in response to a confused listener. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Use this supplied brief speech excerpt: “Our school discards usable paper every day. Last week, volunteers counted twelve full recycling bins but seven classroom trash cans containing clean paper. A labeled paper-reuse station in each hallway would make the better choice visible and easy. I am asking the student council to fund three stations for a four-week pilot.” Submit: a 400–500-word communication analysis. Include: speaker, intended audience, message, channel, two possible forms of noise, one feedback method, general and specific purpose, and one ethical responsibility concerning the numerical claim. Evaluation: The teacher checks correct use of the communication model, evidence-based interpretation of the excerpt, practical feedback, and ethical handling of claims.

modules.title: Managing Speech Anxiety
modules.objectives: Identify physiological and psychological symptoms of communication apprehension; apply cognitive restructuring and physical relaxation techniques; use systematic desensitization strategies to reduce speech anxiety.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §3.3 for preparation, cognitive restructuring, relaxation, and gradual practice; then OpenStax §19.7 https://openstax.org/books/writing-guide/pages/19-7-spotlight-on-delivery-public-speaking for rate, volume, posture, gesture, and eye contact. Kinesics is the study of body movement in nonverbal communication, including gesture, posture, and facial expression. Communication apprehension is fear about anticipated or actual communication; sympathetic arousal can include a racing heart and sweating. Cognitive restructuring replaces catastrophic self-talk with a realistic alternative: “One pause does not erase my preparation.” Comfortable slow diaphragmatic breathing with an unforced longer exhale can help manage arousal. In ordinary classroom coaching, a desensitization-style hierarchy pairs relaxation with gradually more challenging rehearsals; it is not a promise to cure anxiety.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Managing Speech Anxiety. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Worked rehearsal ladder: first read a neutral 60-second explanation alone, then deliver it from keywords to a recording, then deliver a revised version to a recording or willing listener. Progress at a manageable pace. Try 130–160 words per minute as an initial coaching target, then adjust for clarity and language; it is not a universal ideal. Count spoken words/time rather than inventing an improvement. Practice purposeful pauses, three gaze zones, and gestures that illustrate the message. Persistent distress can be raised with a trusted adult; no personal anxiety disclosure is required. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Use this fictional speaker profile: Riley reports tension 8/10 before speaking, speaks 175 words per minute during rehearsal, avoids eye contact, and has practiced only once. Submit: a one-week preparation plan plus a 250–350-word rationale. Include: three timed practice sessions, a two-minute breathing or grounding routine, one cognitive reframe, a target speaking-rate range, a plan for eye contact using three room zones, and a before/after measurement table. For Riley, distinguish proposed targets from supplied baseline facts; do not fabricate outcomes. Do not diagnose Riley or require personal anxiety disclosure. Evaluation: The teacher checks that each strategy addresses supplied evidence, targets are measurable, practice progresses gradually, and claims stay within ordinary performance coaching. Oral component within this assignment: adapt the supplied M1 paper-reuse excerpt into three 60-second spoken explanations, adding only clearly labeled reasoning rather than new factual claims following the gradual practice ladder. Use a private recording or a teacher-observed live delivery; a public audience is not required. Submit one recording or the teacher’s observation checklist, plus a rehearsal log with actual duration, words per minute, one specific observation about pauses/clarity, one revision, and the result of trying that revision. Do not equate the fictional Riley ratings with your own health. Evaluation also checks completion of oral practice, observable evidence, and whether the revision responds to the recorded or observed feedback.

modules.title: Audience Analysis
modules.objectives: Conduct demographic and psychographic audience analysis; explain how audience knowledge, attitudes, and values affect speech design; adapt a speech's language, examples, and appeals to a specific audience.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §5.2 for demographic, psychological, and situational audience analysis. Demographic information concerns group characteristics such as age or education; psychographic information concerns values, beliefs, attitudes, and interests. Demographic patterns do not reveal any individual’s beliefs, gender identity, or culture from appearance. Situational analysis concerns occasion, group size, venue, and time. Verify relevant assumptions respectfully. With a resistant audience, establish shared concerns, acknowledge objections, and present evidence without treating disagreement as ignorance.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Audience Analysis. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Worked adaptation: students may need a plain explanation of staffing costs; administrators may need a staffing and supervision plan. Both can value safe study space. Practice: write “likely concern” and “evidence still needed” separately for each audience, adapt one opening for each, and keep the proposal and facts consistent. Neither audience profile establishes unanimous opinion. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Prepare the same two-minute proposal—extend the school library by one hour—for two fictional audiences: (A) students who support the idea but know little about staffing costs, and (B) administrators concerned about supervision and budget. Submit: a two-column audience-analysis chart and two adapted opening paragraphs. Include: prior knowledge, likely attitude, stakes, one question each audience may ask, evidence each needs, appropriate tone, and one assumption you must verify. Evaluation: The teacher checks meaningful adaptation between audiences, alignment of evidence and tone, explicit assumptions, and consistent core purpose.

modules.title: Topic Selection & Purpose
modules.objectives: Distinguish among general purpose, specific purpose, and central idea; select an appropriate speech topic using brainstorming and narrowing strategies; write a clear specific purpose statement and central idea. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §6.4 for the infinitive convention, and the purpose-planning model in OpenStax §19.5 https://openstax.org/books/writing-guide/pages/19-5-writing-process-writing-to-speak. Two valid specific-purpose forms are “To inform my audience how a rain garden works” and “After my speech, the audience will be able to explain how a rain garden works.” The assignment selects the audience-outcome form; a question may explicitly select the infinitive form. General purpose is the broad aim (inform, persuade, entertain); central idea is the audience-facing claim, such as “Rain gardens slow runoff but need maintenance.” Narrow topic scope to the audience, occasion, and speaking time. Correction for the assigned §19.5 model: its bottle statistic changes from “per day” in the introduction to “per year” in the conclusion. Treat that as an unresolved unit inconsistency; do not copy or convert the statistic as verified evidence without an original source.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Topic Selection & Purpose. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Read §17.2 on claims of fact, value, and policy. Worked distinctions: “The pilot reduced discarded bottles” is a factual claim needing data; “Reducing avoidable waste is responsible” is a value judgment needing criteria; “The council should fund the pilot” is a policy proposal. Practice: convert one purpose between both valid forms, then write a separate central idea. A purpose names a desired response; a central idea states the message, not merely “to inform.” Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Choose one of these bounded topics: add a shaded outdoor study area, start a device-free lunch table, or create a peer tutoring hour. Submit: a topic-narrowing worksheet and a 250–350-word rationale. Include: general purpose, specific purpose in “After my speech, the audience will…” form, one-sentence central idea, audience, occasion, three main points, a scope boundary, evidence supporting one proposed main point, and one ethical risk such as overclaiming benefits. Evaluation: The teacher checks alignment among topic, audience, purpose, central idea, and main points, plus a realistic scope for a three-minute speech.

modules.title: Research & Supporting Material
modules.objectives: Identify major types of supporting material (examples, statistics, testimony, definitions); evaluate the credibility of oral sources; use statistics ethically and effectively in speeches.
modules.readingNote: Read §19.5 for evidence-based speech drafting and the source cards below for practice. Reading correction for OpenStax §19.5: its bottle statistic switches from “per day” in the introduction to “per year” in the conclusion. This is an unresolved unit inconsistency; do not copy it as verified evidence or convert it without an original source. Distinguish a brief example from an extended narrative, a definition from evidence of causes, and relevant expert testimony from celebrity endorsement. An oral citation should identify the author or conducting organization, title/publication, date, and relevant method or limit. Ethos concerns credibility and goodwill, logos concerns reasoning and evidence, and pathos concerns emotion; none licenses misleading claims.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Research & Supporting Material. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §7.3 for spoken source identification. Worked source-card calculation: 2 extra hours/day × 2 additional staff total × $38/hour × 5 days/week = $760/week in additional staffing costs; two additional staff at each of two libraries would instead cost $1,520/week. Survey response rate is 120/850 ≈ 14.12%; 72/120 = 60% of respondents said yes, not 72% of all students. Practice: identify the denominator, time unit, source organization, and voluntary-sample limit in each quantitative claim. The separate quiz’s hypothetical 72% is not the source-card result. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Evaluate these supplied simulated source cards for a speech on later library hours: (1) “Spring Access and Staffing Review,” Jordan Lee, district operations director, April 12, 2025: door-counter and overtime-log data from two high-school libraries for eight spring weeks; keeping both libraries open two extra hours per day on five school days per week would require two additional staff total (one per library, alongside existing adult coverage) at $38 per hour, or $760 per week in additional staffing costs; this is not the total supervision budget; summer and exam weeks were not studied. (2) Anonymous @StudyLate post, April 20, 2025: “Everyone stays late, so the library should too”; no method or supporting data. (3) District Student Council voluntary online survey, April 2025: emailed to 850 students; 120 responded to “Would you use the school library after 5 p.m. at least once per week?”; 72 yes, 30 maybe, 18 no; respondents self-selected. (4) Recorded interview by Maya Chen with librarian Priya Shah, May 2, 2025: Shah has six years of district experience and says evening access needs at least two adults plus an administrator emergency contact; the interview does not independently establish cost or student demand. Submit: a four-row credibility table and a 350–450-word evidence plan. Include: authority, currency, method, possible bias, the claim each source can support, one claim it cannot support, and how you would cite it orally. Evaluation: The teacher checks source-claim fit, recognition of sampling limits, balanced use of quantitative and qualitative evidence, and complete oral-citation elements.

modules.title: Organizing a Speech
modules.objectives: Apply five organizational patterns for speeches (topical, chronological, spatial, problem-solution, Monroe's Motivated Sequence); select the pattern most appropriate for a given speech purpose; use main points and subpoints effectively. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §10.2 for topical (categories), chronological (time or process steps), spatial (location), and problem-solution organization. Read §17.3 https://saylordotorg.github.io/text_stand-up-speak-out-the-practice-and-ethics-of-public-speaking/s20-03-organizing-persuasive-speeches.html for Monroe’s sequence: Attention gains interest; Need establishes the problem; Satisfaction proposes a remedy; Visualization depicts realistic consequences; Action asks for a specific next step. A demonstration whose steps depend on earlier steps normally uses chronological order. Main points are coordinate ideas; indented subpoints support their parent point; transitions link sections. For the sleep assignment, treat the supplied idea cards as packet claims, not independently verified research findings.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Organizing a Speech. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Reading correction for OpenStax §19.5: its bottle statistic switches from “per day” in the introduction to “per year” in the conclusion. This is an unresolved unit inconsistency; do not copy it as verified evidence or convert it without an original source. Worked Monroe model using a hypothetical reuse pilot: ask about wasted paper (Attention), identify clean paper in trash (Need), propose stations (Satisfaction), describe a possible tidier reuse process without inventing a measured benefit (Visualization), and request a four-week pilot vote (Action). Practice: contrast this action-oriented sequence with an informative three-category explanation, then rehearse a clear transition between two points. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Organize these idea cards for an informative speech about school sleep: biological clock shifts in adolescence; screen light can delay sleep timing; early schedules reduce sleep opportunity; insufficient sleep affects attention; consistent routines can help; individual needs vary. Submit: a preparation outline using one justified organizational pattern and a 250–350-word rationale. Include: central idea, three parallel main points, supporting evidence cards under each point, transitions, internal previews or summaries, and an explanation of why the chosen pattern is clearer than one alternative. Evaluation: The teacher checks logical hierarchy, parallel wording, placement of support, transition quality, and fit between pattern, audience, and purpose. Oral component within this assignment: deliver a 90-second version from the outline to a private recording or the teacher. Identify one unclear transition through replay or teacher feedback, revise it, and redeliver that section. Include the recording or teacher checklist and the before/after transition in the submission. Evaluation also checks whether spoken transitions make the chosen structure audible.

modules.title: Introductions & Conclusions
modules.objectives: Write a speech introduction using an effective attention-getter, audience motivation, credibility statement, and preview; craft a conclusion that signals the end, summarizes main points, and ends memorably. Students will analyze model texts, draft or revise written responses, and support claims with textual evidence in the module assignment.
modules.readingNote: Read §19.5 for openings and closings. Reading correction for OpenStax §19.5: its bottle statistic switches from “per day” in the introduction to “per year” in the conclusion. This is an unresolved unit inconsistency; do not copy it as verified evidence or convert it without an original source. A useful introduction gains attention, establishes audience relevance and speaker credibility, states the central idea, and previews points. A rhetorical question invites thought without requiring an aloud response. A conclusion signals closure, summarizes, and uses a memorable clincher or appropriate action request without adding new unsupported arguments. An internal summary reviews a section; an internal preview forecasts the next one.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Introductions & Conclusions. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §18.2 for ceremonial forms. A tribute honors a person or group through relevant qualities and contributions; a how-to demonstration explains a procedure, and a persuasive speech seeks a belief or action. Worked fictional tribute: “Our library volunteers kept the reading corner welcoming by repairing worn books and greeting new readers.” Practice: name the contribution and shared value, then distinguish this tribute from a request to fund the library. For the bottle assignment, use the supplied pilot goal without inventing a waste statistic. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Use this central idea: “A four-week reusable-bottle pilot can reduce single-use waste while giving the school evidence before a permanent decision.” Submit: two alternative introductions and two alternative conclusions for a three-minute proposal. Each introduction must include an attention device, audience relevance, speaker credibility, central idea, and preview; each conclusion must signal closure, summarize the points, and end with a specific call to action. Include: a 200–300-word comparison explaining which pair best fits a skeptical school committee and why. Evaluation: The teacher checks completeness, consistency with the central idea, ethical tone, audience fit, and a conclusion that does not introduce a new argument.

modules.title: Outlining
modules.objectives: Distinguish between preparation outlines and speaking outlines; create a complete preparation outline with citations; construct a keyword speaking outline for use during delivery.
modules.readingNote: Read Stand Up, Speak Out §12.2 for full preparation outlines and concise speaking outlines; also OpenStax §19.5 https://openstax.org/books/writing-guide/pages/19-5-writing-process-writing-to-speak. Reading correction for OpenStax §19.5: its bottle statistic switches from “per day” in the introduction to “per year” in the conclusion. This is an unresolved unit inconsistency; do not copy it as verified evidence or convert it without an original source. Preparation outlines use full-sentence points, subordinate evidence, and full source details; speaking outlines retain keywords, brief source cues, timing, and delivery reminders. Parallel points use matching grammatical form. A keyword outline supports rehearsal, not reading a manuscript. Supplemental STAR practice: Situation gives context, Task gives responsibility, Action states what the speaker did, and Result reports an evidenced outcome. Fictional model: a club display was delayed (S); I had to organize setup (T); I assigned tasks and checked progress (A); setup finished before opening (R). Do not invent a result for a real experience.
modules.videoNote: GIIS lesson video — Outlining. Watch this lesson before completing the module assignment.
modules.practiceNote: Read the text of the Assertion-Evidence tutorial, steps 2–4; films, downloads, and external quizzes are not required. A sentence headline asserts a claim and a diagram or graph provides visual support. For the supplied packet, “A rain garden slows runoff through a planted basin” can head a labeled inlet–basin–overflow diagram. CRAP design checks are Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, and Proximity: emphasize the route, repeat label styles, align labels, and place each beside its feature. Dense verbatim slide prose read aloud over a visual can compete for processing; short labels and accessibility captions serve different needs, so redundancy is not always harmful. Practice: replace a paragraph with a claim, diagram, and brief labels; then use pauses, audience scanning, and purposeful movement in delivery. Reflect on observed improvement and a next goal. Use the supplied assignment packet; no paid practice service or public posting is required.
modules.assignment: Create both a preparation outline and a one-page speaking outline for a two-minute informative talk using this content packet: topic—how a campus rain garden works; process—roof runoff enters a shallow planted basin, soil and roots slow and filter water, overflow exits through a drain; limits—it does not remove every pollutant and requires maintenance. Submit: both outlines and a 200–300-word design note. Include: source cues identifying the supplied classroom content packet (author/date not provided; no claim of independent verification), full-sentence main points in the preparation outline, keywords and delivery cues in the speaking outline, transitions, timing marks, and one planned visual. Evaluation: The teacher checks hierarchy, factual fidelity to the packet, difference between outline types, usable delivery cues, and timing appropriate to two minutes. Oral component within this assignment: rehearse and deliver the complete two-minute talk from the keyword outline with the planned visual, using a private recording or teacher-observed live delivery. Submit the recording or teacher’s observation checklist with the outlines. Replay it or use teacher feedback to log actual duration and two specific observations about clarity, pacing, gaze/gestures, or visual use; revise the outline and redeliver one improved 30–60-second section. In the design note, compare the original and revised delivery and set one measurable next goal. Evaluation also checks audible organization, evidence of using keywords rather than reading a manuscript, purposeful visual/delivery choices, and a revision linked to an observed problem. No public upload or personal story is required.

quizQuestions.question: The communication process model includes all of the following components EXCEPT:
options: Sender and receiver
Message and channel
Noise and feedback
Syntax and semantics only
quizQuestions.answer: Syntax and semantics only
quizQuestions.explanation: The communication process model includes sender, receiver, message, channel, noise, feedback, and context—not just syntax and semantics.

quizQuestions.question: Ethical public speaking requires speakers to:
options: Use any persuasive technique to achieve the desired audience response
Be honest, prepare thoroughly, and respect audience diversity
Speak only about topics they have personal experience with
Avoid using any emotional appeals in their speeches
quizQuestions.answer: Be honest, prepare thoroughly, and respect audience diversity
quizQuestions.explanation: Ethical speakers demonstrate honesty, diligence in preparation, respect for their audience, and responsible use of evidence and persuasive appeals.

quizQuestions.question: During a speech, an audience member looks confused and the speaker restates the main point with an example. In the communication model, the confused expression functions as:
options: Channel
Feedback
Semantic noise
The original message
quizQuestions.answer: Feedback
quizQuestions.explanation: The audience response gives the speaker information about how the message is being received, allowing an immediate adjustment.

quizQuestions.question: Communication apprehension (CA) is best defined as:
options: The physical exhaustion speakers feel after long speeches
An individual's level of fear or anxiety associated with real or anticipated communication
The difficulty speakers experience choosing the right words
Audience disinterest that discourages the speaker during delivery
quizQuestions.answer: An individual's level of fear or anxiety associated with real or anticipated communication
quizQuestions.explanation: Communication apprehension (James McCroskey's concept) describes anxiety about communication situations, which affects speaking performance.

quizQuestions.question: Cognitive restructuring helps speakers manage speech anxiety by:
options: Practicing the speech until memorized word for word
Replacing negative self-talk with realistic, positive thoughts about speaking
Breathing deeply immediately before beginning the speech
Avoiding all public speaking situations to prevent anxiety
quizQuestions.answer: Replacing negative self-talk with realistic, positive thoughts about speaking
quizQuestions.explanation: Cognitive restructuring involves identifying irrational negative thoughts about speaking (e.g., 'I will fail completely') and replacing them with realistic, balanced ones.

quizQuestions.question: The 'fight-or-flight' response experienced during speech anxiety is caused by:
options: Lack of preparation and insufficient practice time
The sympathetic nervous system releasing adrenaline in response to perceived threat
The speaker's inability to remember the speech content
Poor audience feedback during the previous speech
quizQuestions.answer: The sympathetic nervous system releasing adrenaline in response to perceived threat
quizQuestions.explanation: The fight-or-flight response is a physiological reaction to perceived threat, releasing adrenaline that causes symptoms such as increased heart rate and sweating.

quizQuestions.question: Which breathing pattern is most useful for lowering physical arousal immediately before a speech?
options: Slow diaphragmatic breathing with a relaxed, longer exhale
Rapid shallow breathing high in the chest
Holding the breath until the introduction begins
Repeatedly tensing the shoulders while inhaling
quizQuestions.answer: Slow diaphragmatic breathing with a relaxed, longer exhale
quizQuestions.explanation: Slow diaphragmatic breathing and a longer, relaxed exhale can reduce physiological arousal without depriving the speaker of air.

quizQuestions.question: Demographic audience analysis focuses on:
options: The audience's psychological attitudes and values about the topic
Observable characteristics such as age, gender, education, and cultural background
The audience's knowledge of the speaker's credentials
The physical characteristics of the speaking environment
quizQuestions.answer: Observable characteristics such as age, gender, education, and cultural background
quizQuestions.explanation: Demographic analysis examines measurable group characteristics that help speakers anticipate audience needs, expectations, and prior knowledge.

quizQuestions.question: Psychographic audience analysis examines:
options: The average income and education level of audience members
The audience's values, beliefs, attitudes, and lifestyle characteristics
The number of people expected to attend the presentation
Seating arrangement and room configuration
quizQuestions.answer: The audience's values, beliefs, attitudes, and lifestyle characteristics
quizQuestions.explanation: Psychographic analysis goes beyond demographics to understand what the audience believes, values, and cares about, which informs how a speaker frames arguments.

quizQuestions.question: Adapting a speech for a hostile audience (one that disagrees with your position) requires speakers to:
options: Avoid presenting any evidence to prevent further disagreement
Present only emotional appeals and avoid logical arguments
Establish common ground, acknowledge the opposing view, and present evidence carefully
Begin with the strongest arguments and ignore audience resistance
quizQuestions.answer: Establish common ground, acknowledge the opposing view, and present evidence carefully
quizQuestions.explanation: With hostile audiences, speakers should begin by establishing shared values, show respect for the opposing view, and introduce evidence gradually to avoid triggering defensive reactions.

quizQuestions.question: Under the infinitive-phrase convention for planning a specific purpose, which description is correct?
options: A one-sentence preview of the speech's three main points
A single infinitive phrase stating precisely what the speaker wants the audience to know, feel, or do
The topic narrowed to a single paragraph summary
The central idea restated as a question
quizQuestions.answer: A single infinitive phrase stating precisely what the speaker wants the audience to know, feel, or do
quizQuestions.explanation: The selected convention begins with “To inform/persuade…” and names the desired audience response. An audience-outcome sentence is also valid and is the convention required in the M4 assignment; a central idea states the message itself.

quizQuestions.question: The central idea (thesis) of a speech differs from the specific purpose in that the central idea:
options: Is stated only in the speaker's notes, not in the speech itself
Is the speaker's goal stated as an infinitive phrase
States the core claim or message of the speech in a complete sentence for the audience
Lists all three main points as separate sentences
quizQuestions.answer: States the core claim or message of the speech in a complete sentence for the audience
quizQuestions.explanation: The central idea is stated aloud in the speech for the audience to hear; the specific purpose is the speaker's goal statement used in planning.

quizQuestions.question: The three general purposes for public speeches are:
options: To analyze, to criticize, and to evaluate
To entertain, to enlighten, and to empower
To inform, to persuade, and to entertain
To report, to argue, and to celebrate
quizQuestions.answer: To inform, to persuade, and to entertain
quizQuestions.explanation: The three classical general purposes for speeches are informing (increasing audience understanding), persuading (influencing beliefs or actions), and entertaining (providing enjoyment).

quizQuestions.question: Which factor is most important when selecting a speech topic?
options: Choosing the most obscure topic to appear intellectually sophisticated
Selecting a topic the speaker knows about, cares about, and that is appropriate for the audience and occasion
Using a topic assigned by a previous instructor in another class
Choosing the longest topic available to maximize research opportunities
quizQuestions.answer: Selecting a topic the speaker knows about, cares about, and that is appropriate for the audience and occasion
quizQuestions.explanation: The best topics combine the speaker's genuine interest and knowledge with audience relevance and situational appropriateness.

quizQuestions.question: Expert testimony as a type of supporting material is most credible when:
options: The expert is a celebrity with a large social media following
The expert has recognized credentials and expertise in the relevant field
The expert agrees exactly with the speaker's conclusion
The expert's testimony is the most recent available on the topic
quizQuestions.answer: The expert has recognized credentials and expertise in the relevant field
quizQuestions.explanation: Expert testimony is credible when the source has verifiable credentials, training, or experience directly relevant to the claim being supported.

quizQuestions.question: A brief example in a speech is characterized by:
options: A detailed narrative story illustrating a single point
A specific instance or case mentioned in one or two sentences
Statistical data drawn from multiple research studies
A hypothetical scenario presented as if it actually happened
quizQuestions.answer: A specific instance or case mentioned in one or two sentences
quizQuestions.explanation: Brief examples are short, specific instances used to quickly illustrate a point without extended narration.

quizQuestions.question: A hypothetical District Student Council survey has 120 voluntary respondents and about 72% support. Which oral citation identifies the organization and sampling limit without overgeneralizing?
options: “The District Student Council’s March 2025 survey proves about 72% of all students support the pilot, based on 120 volunteers.”
“A March 2025 Pilot Preference Survey found about 72% support among 120 voluntary respondents.”
“The District Student Council’s March 2025 Pilot Preference Survey found about 72% support among 120 voluntary respondents.”
“The District Student Council’s March 2025 survey found about 72% support among 120 randomly selected respondents.”
quizQuestions.answer: “The District Student Council’s March 2025 Pilot Preference Survey found about 72% support among 120 voluntary respondents.”
quizQuestions.explanation: This version names the conducting organization, survey title, date, respondent count, result, and voluntary sampling. It still does not supply invitations or response rate and cannot establish school-wide support. This separate hypothetical result is not the assignment’s 72-of-120 result (60%).

quizQuestions.question: A speaker defines “food insecurity” with a published operational definition before presenting local statistics. What is the definition mainly helping the audience do?
options: Interpret the statistics using a clear, consistent meaning
Assume the local sample represents every community
Treat the definition as expert testimony about causes
Replace the need to identify the data source
quizQuestions.answer: Interpret the statistics using a clear, consistent meaning
quizQuestions.explanation: An operational definition specifies how a term is used or measured, so listeners can interpret later evidence consistently.

quizQuestions.question: The chronological organizational pattern is best suited for speeches that:
options: Compare two or more different positions on an issue
Present information according to time sequence or historical development
Divide a topic into categories of equal importance
Move from a problem statement to a proposed solution
quizQuestions.answer: Present information according to time sequence or historical development
quizQuestions.explanation: Chronological organization arranges information in time order—useful for explaining historical events, processes, or biographical narratives.

quizQuestions.question: Monroe's Motivated Sequence is primarily used for:
options: Informative speeches explaining scientific processes
Ceremonial speeches at weddings and graduations
Persuasive speeches designed to motivate specific audience action
Introductory speeches at professional conferences
quizQuestions.answer: Persuasive speeches designed to motivate specific audience action
quizQuestions.explanation: Monroe's Motivated Sequence (Attention, Need, Satisfaction, Visualization, Action) is specifically designed to move audiences from awareness of a problem to taking action.

quizQuestions.question: The problem-solution organizational pattern works best when:
options: The speech aims to entertain the audience with a humorous narrative
The speaker wants to describe a geographic location or physical space
The speaker identifies a significant problem and proposes a course of action to address it
The speech compares the advantages and disadvantages of two options
quizQuestions.answer: The speaker identifies a significant problem and proposes a course of action to address it
quizQuestions.explanation: Problem-solution organization first establishes that a significant problem exists, then proposes and justifies a specific solution.

quizQuestions.question: A speech has three main points: neighborhood parks, school recreation spaces, and indoor community centers. Which organizational pattern does this use?
options: Topical order
Chronological order
Problem-solution order
Monroe’s Motivated Sequence
quizQuestions.answer: Topical order
quizQuestions.explanation: Topical organization divides a subject into coordinate categories rather than arranging points by time, place, or a persuasion sequence.

quizQuestions.question: The credibility statement in a speech introduction is designed to:
options: List all the sources cited in the speech
Establish the speaker's qualification or connection to the topic
Preview the main points of the speech
Thank the audience for their time before beginning
quizQuestions.answer: Establish the speaker's qualification or connection to the topic
quizQuestions.explanation: The credibility statement tells the audience why they should trust the speaker on this particular topic—relevant experience, research, or personal connection.

quizQuestions.question: A rhetorical question used as an attention-getter in a speech is effective because:
options: It requires audience members to answer aloud, creating participation
It engages audience thinking without requiring a formal response
It demonstrates the speaker's knowledge of the topic immediately
It provides the statistical evidence the speech will discuss
quizQuestions.answer: It engages audience thinking without requiring a formal response
quizQuestions.explanation: A rhetorical question invites the audience to mentally consider an answer, immediately drawing them into the topic without requiring verbal participation.

quizQuestions.question: A speaker ends the causes section with “We have seen why flooding is increasing; next, we will compare two solutions.” This sentence is primarily a:
options: Transition with an internal summary and preview
Credibility statement
Rhetorical question
Specific-purpose statement
quizQuestions.answer: Transition with an internal summary and preview
quizQuestions.explanation: The sentence closes one section, names what has been covered, and previews the next section, helping listeners follow the shift.

quizQuestions.question: A speaking outline differs from a preparation outline in that a speaking outline:
options: Contains complete sentences and full source citations
Contains keyword phrases to guide delivery without reading word for word
Is submitted to the instructor for grading
Must follow the same format as the preparation outline exactly
quizQuestions.answer: Contains keyword phrases to guide delivery without reading word for word
quizQuestions.explanation: A speaking outline is a condensed version with keywords and cues—not complete sentences—that allows the speaker to refer to notes while maintaining eye contact and natural delivery.

quizQuestions.question: Proper subordination in an outline means that:
options: All items are placed at the same indentation level
Subpoints are indented under main points and contain narrower, supporting content
The main points are listed alphabetically
Sources are listed before the speech content they support
quizQuestions.answer: Subpoints are indented under main points and contain narrower, supporting content
quizQuestions.explanation: Subordination ensures that subpoints (supporting details) are hierarchically organized under main points, visually and logically indicating their supporting relationship.

quizQuestions.question: A preparation outline serves which primary purpose?
options: To be read aloud verbatim during the speech delivery
To help the speaker plan, organize, and check the logic of the speech before rehearsal
To substitute for practice by providing a complete script
To be distributed to audience members so they can follow along
quizQuestions.answer: To help the speaker plan, organize, and check the logic of the speech before rehearsal
quizQuestions.explanation: A preparation outline is a planning tool that ensures the speech's argument is logically organized, properly supported, and complete before the speaker begins rehearsing delivery.

quizQuestions.question: Which pair of main points uses parallel grammatical form?
options: I. Reducing cafeteria waste; II. Expanding food-donation partnerships
I. Causes of cafeteria waste; II. How the school can donate food
I. The waste problem; II. Students will organize donations
I. Why food is discarded; II. A partnership with shelters
quizQuestions.answer: I. Reducing cafeteria waste; II. Expanding food-donation partnerships
quizQuestions.explanation: Both points use matching gerund phrases, making coordinate ideas easier for a speaker and audience to track.

questions.question: In the communication process model, 'channel' refers to:
options: The speaker's emotional state during delivery
The medium through which a message is transmitted (voice, video, text)
The feedback received from the audience
The physical environment where communication takes place
questions.answer: The medium through which a message is transmitted (voice, video, text)
questions.explanation: The channel is the pathway or medium through which a message travels from sender to receiver—face-to-face voice, video, written text, etc.

questions.question: Cognitive restructuring as a speech anxiety management technique involves:
options: Practicing deep breathing immediately before speaking
Replacing irrational negative self-talk with realistic positive thoughts
Memorizing the speech completely to reduce uncertainty
Avoiding high-stakes speaking situations
questions.answer: Replacing irrational negative self-talk with realistic positive thoughts
questions.explanation: Cognitive restructuring targets the thought patterns that drive anxiety—replacing catastrophic thinking with balanced, realistic self-assessment.

questions.question: Demographic audience analysis examines which type of variables?
options: The audience's values, beliefs, and lifestyle preferences
Observable group characteristics like age, gender, and education level
The psychological barriers to persuasion in the audience
The physical layout and technical setup of the speaking venue
questions.answer: Observable group characteristics like age, gender, and education level
questions.explanation: Demographic variables are measurable group characteristics that help speakers anticipate audience background, prior knowledge, and expectations.

questions.question: Which statement uses the infinitive convention for a specific purpose taught in M4?
options: To inform my audience how a rain garden slows runoff
After my speech, the audience will explain how a rain garden slows runoff
Rain gardens slow runoff through soil and roots
To inform
questions.answer: To inform my audience how a rain garden slows runoff
questions.explanation: The first is a specific infinitive goal. The audience-outcome sentence is another valid convention but not the one requested. The declarative claim is a central idea; “To inform” alone is only a general purpose.

questions.question: Expert testimony as supporting material is credible primarily when:
options: The expert is popular on social media platforms
The expert has verifiable credentials and expertise in the relevant field
The expert's view agrees exactly with the speaker's argument
The expert was cited in a Wikipedia article
questions.answer: The expert has verifiable credentials and expertise in the relevant field
questions.explanation: Expert testimony gains credibility from the source's recognized expertise, qualifications, and institutional standing in the relevant field.

questions.question: Monroe's Motivated Sequence is most appropriate for which type of speech?
options: An informative speech explaining a scientific concept
A commemorative speech honoring a historical figure
A persuasive speech designed to motivate audience action
An introductory speech at a professional conference
questions.answer: A persuasive speech designed to motivate audience action
questions.explanation: Monroe's Motivated Sequence moves audiences from attention through need, satisfaction, visualization, to action—making it ideal for action-oriented persuasive speeches.

questions.question: The preview statement in a speech introduction is designed to:
options: Provide detailed evidence for the first main point
Briefly identify the main points the speech will address
Establish the speaker's qualifications on the topic
Create suspense by withholding the speech's central argument
questions.answer: Briefly identify the main points the speech will address
questions.explanation: The preview gives the audience a roadmap—a brief statement of the main points in the order they will be presented.

questions.question: Which feature belongs primarily in a speaking outline rather than a full preparation outline?
options: Concise keywords, brief source cues, and pause reminders
Complete sentences explaining each supporting argument
Full bibliographic entries for every cited source
A complete word-for-word manuscript for reading aloud
questions.answer: Concise keywords, brief source cues, and pause reminders
questions.explanation: M8: a speaking outline is condensed for delivery and eye contact. Detailed sentences and full citations support preparation; a verbatim manuscript is a different delivery aid.

questions.question: Oral style in public speaking differs from written style in that oral style typically features:
options: Longer, more complex sentence structures
Passive voice for formal and objective tone
Shorter sentences, direct language, and repetition for listener comprehension
Technical jargon and discipline-specific vocabulary
questions.answer: Shorter sentences, direct language, and repetition for listener comprehension
questions.explanation: Spoken language must be immediately understood by listeners who cannot re-read—so oral style uses simpler, more direct, and repetitive structures.

questions.question: Kinesics in nonverbal communication refers to:
options: The use of physical space and distance between communicators
The vocal pitch, rate, and volume used by a speaker
Body movements, gestures, posture, and facial expressions
The physical setting and environmental context of communication
questions.answer: Body movements, gestures, posture, and facial expressions
questions.explanation: Kinesics is the study of body movement—including gesture, posture, and facial expression—as nonverbal communication.

questions.question: The CRAP design principles for visual aids include all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Contrast
Repetition
Alignment
Creativity
questions.answer: Creativity
questions.explanation: CRAP stands for Contrast, Repetition, Alignment, and Proximity—not Creativity. These four principles guide professional visual design.

questions.question: Which purpose is primarily informative?
options: Explain how soil and roots slow runoff in a rain garden
Urge the council to fund a rain garden next semester
Honor a volunteer for maintaining the school garden
Argue that garden volunteering is morally admirable
questions.answer: Explain how soil and roots slow runoff in a rain garden
questions.explanation: Explaining a process increases understanding. Funding seeks policy action, honoring a volunteer is ceremonial, and moral evaluation argues a value claim.

questions.question: Aristotle's three artistic proofs (appeals) for persuasion are:
options: Facts, opinions, and testimonials
Ethos, logos, and pathos
Induction, deduction, and analogy
Authority, popularity, and tradition
questions.answer: Ethos, logos, and pathos
questions.explanation: Aristotle identified ethos (credibility), logos (logic), and pathos (emotion) as the three primary means of persuasion in rhetoric.

questions.question: The topical organizational pattern for speeches organizes content by:
options: Time sequence from earliest to most recent event
Logical categories or subtopics of the main subject
Geographic movement from one location to another
A problem followed by its proposed solution
questions.answer: Logical categories or subtopics of the main subject
questions.explanation: Topical organization divides a topic into its natural subcategories when chronological, spatial, or problem-solution structures are not appropriate.

questions.question: Communication apprehension affects public speakers most significantly through:
options: Making them speak too slowly for effective communication
Generating anxiety that can interfere with preparation, delivery, and performance
Reducing the quality of research and supporting material gathered
Causing them to select inappropriate organizational patterns
questions.answer: Generating anxiety that can interfere with preparation, delivery, and performance
questions.explanation: Communication apprehension creates anxiety that can disrupt the speaker's preparation process, cognitive functioning during delivery, and overall performance quality.

questions.question: Which rehearsal plan best illustrates a desensitization-style approach to ordinary speech anxiety?
options: Practice manageable speaking steps with relaxation, gradually increasing the challenge
Start with the largest possible audience before any rehearsal
Use breathing exercises but postpone every speaking attempt
Memorize silently and avoid practicing aloud
questions.answer: Practice manageable speaking steps with relaxation, gradually increasing the challenge
questions.explanation: M2 combines gradual speaking practice with relaxation. Sudden maximum challenge skips the hierarchy; breathing alone and silent memorization omit graduated speaking exposure. Classroom practice does not guarantee a clinical outcome.

questions.question: Adapting a speech for a hostile audience requires the speaker to:
options: Begin with the most aggressive arguments to establish dominance
Establish common ground, show respect for the opposing view, and introduce evidence carefully
Avoid presenting any statistics that could be disputed
Skip the introduction and begin directly with the strongest evidence
questions.answer: Establish common ground, show respect for the opposing view, and introduce evidence carefully
questions.explanation: With hostile audiences, credibility and relationship-building must come first—common ground reduces defensiveness and creates openness to the argument.

questions.question: A speech of tribute is a special occasion speech designed to:
options: Inform the audience about a topic the speaker researched
Honor and recognize a person's qualities, contributions, and achievements
Persuade the audience to support a political or social cause
Demonstrate a complex skill or process step by step
questions.answer: Honor and recognize a person's qualities, contributions, and achievements
questions.explanation: A speech of tribute celebrates and honors a person or group, highlighting their admirable qualities and contributions to inspire and move the audience.

questions.question: The 'Visualization' step in Monroe's Motivated Sequence asks the speaker to:
options: Capture audience attention with a dramatic statistic or story
Propose a specific solution to the problem identified
Help the audience vividly imagine the positive outcome if they act
Call the audience to take immediate specific action
questions.answer: Help the audience vividly imagine the positive outcome if they act
questions.explanation: Visualization projects the audience forward—showing them concretely what their world will look like if they adopt the speaker's proposed solution.

questions.question: Which statement is a persuasive value claim?
options: Reducing avoidable waste is ethically responsible
The cafeteria discarded twenty bottles yesterday
The council should fund three reuse stations
A reuse station holds clean paper on labeled shelves
questions.answer: Reducing avoidable waste is ethically responsible
questions.explanation: M4: a value claim evaluates worth using criteria such as responsibility. A count is a factual claim, a funding recommendation is a policy claim, and the last statement describes an object.

questions.question: Strategic pausing in a speech serves which communicative purpose?
options: It fills empty time when the speaker has forgotten the next point
It creates emphasis, signals importance, and gives audiences time to process
It signals to the audience that the speech is nearing its conclusion
It allows the speaker to check notes without appearing unprepared
questions.answer: It creates emphasis, signals importance, and gives audiences time to process
questions.explanation: Deliberate pauses are powerful delivery tools—they mark important ideas, create dramatic effect, and allow cognitive processing time.

questions.question: The Assertion-Evidence slide design approach uses slide headlines that:
options: Are single keywords identifying the slide's topic
Are complete sentences asserting the slide's key claim
Ask a question the slide's content will answer
List the sources cited on the slide
questions.answer: Are complete sentences asserting the slide's key claim
questions.explanation: Assertion-Evidence slides use headline sentences that state the key claim—even a quick glance conveys the main point without requiring reading the full slide.

questions.question: Ethos as a persuasive appeal is most directly strengthened when a speaker:
options: Uses emotional language to connect with the audience's feelings
Presents extensive statistical data and expert evidence
Demonstrates expertise, trustworthiness, and genuine care for the audience
Organizes the speech in a clear and logical sequence
questions.answer: Demonstrates expertise, trustworthiness, and genuine care for the audience
questions.explanation: Ethos is built through demonstrated competence, reliability, and goodwill—audiences are persuaded by speakers they perceive as knowledgeable, honest, and caring.

questions.question: A demonstration teaches a procedure in which each step must be completed before the next. Which primary order best helps listeners reproduce it?
options: Chronological or step-by-step order
Spatial order from the left side of the room to the right
Topical order grouping all tools before all outcomes
Problem-solution order centered on arguing for a policy change
questions.answer: Chronological or step-by-step order
questions.explanation: M6: dependent procedural steps need an audible sequence. Spatial order tracks location, topical order groups categories, and a policy argument does not itself supply the ordered procedure.

questions.question: Eye contact in public speaking is most effective when the speaker:
options: Fixes their gaze on a single friendly face throughout the speech
Looks at different audience members across all sections of the room
Looks at the back wall to avoid direct contact with individuals
Maintains eye contact only during key statistics and data
questions.answer: Looks at different audience members across all sections of the room
questions.explanation: Effective eye contact is distributed across all audience members, making everyone feel included and creating the sense of genuine conversation.

questions.question: A clincher at the end of a speech should:
options: Introduce new evidence that was not covered in the body
Thank the audience and ask for questions immediately
Provide a memorable final statement that reinforces the central message
Restate the introduction's opening hook word for word
questions.answer: Provide a memorable final statement that reinforces the central message
questions.explanation: A clincher creates a powerful close—whether a callback, call to action, or memorable quote—that leaves the audience with the central message.

questions.question: When adapting language for a public speech compared to a written essay, speakers should:
options: Use more passive voice for objectivity
Use longer, more complex sentences for precision
Use shorter, direct sentences and personal pronouns for clarity
Avoid repetition as it signals poor preparation
questions.answer: Use shorter, direct sentences and personal pronouns for clarity
questions.explanation: Oral style must be immediately comprehensible to listeners—shorter sentences, active voice, and direct address facilitate real-time understanding.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly expands the STAR method taught in M8?
options: Situation, Task, Action, Result
Situation, Theory, Argument, Recommendation
Summary, Task, Analysis, Reflection
Source, Thesis, Audience, Rehearsal
questions.answer: Situation, Task, Action, Result
questions.explanation: STAR first sets context and responsibility, then identifies the speaker’s action and evidenced outcome. Theory/argument, analysis/reflection, and speech-planning elements are different frameworks, not the STAR sequence.

questions.question: When a narrated presentation already explains a visual, adding dense verbatim on-screen prose can:
options: Guarantee twice as much learning through duplication
Reduce processing efficiency as reading competes with following the visual and narration
Make brief labels and all accessibility captions unnecessary
Eliminate the need to explain the visual aloud
questions.answer: Reduce processing efficiency as reading competes with following the visual and narration
questions.explanation: M8: dense duplicated prose can add processing demands when learners must also inspect a visual. This is conditional, not a ban on text: concise labels, captions for accessibility, learner needs, and presentation conditions can change the effect.

questions.question: A capstone reflection at the end of a public speaking course primarily requires students to:
options: Critique the instructor's feedback for accuracy and fairness
Memorize and recite course terminology and definitions
Evaluate their growth as speakers, identify improved skills, and set future goals
Rank themselves against their classmates on each speech assignment
questions.answer: Evaluate their growth as speakers, identify improved skills, and set future goals
questions.explanation: A capstone reflection requires metacognitive self-assessment—honest evaluation of improvement, recognition of remaining challenges, and forward-looking goal setting.

questions.question: Motivated movement in a speech is defined as:
options: Random pacing back and forth that signals nervousness
Physical movement that serves a communicative purpose during delivery
Moving behind a podium to signal the beginning of the speech
Movement used only during the introduction and conclusion
questions.answer: Physical movement that serves a communicative purpose during delivery
questions.explanation: Motivated movement is intentional—moving toward the audience for emphasis, stepping to a new position to signal transitions, or gesturing to reinforce key points.

questions.question: An audience looks confused during a technical explanation. Which response best checks understanding and adapts to that feedback?
options: Pause, restate the idea plainly, offer an example, and check whether it helped
Increase volume while repeating the same unexplained terminology
Skip the explanation and proceed directly to the conclusion
Add several new technical terms to make the explanation more precise
questions.answer: Pause, restate the idea plainly, offer an example, and check whether it helped
questions.explanation: M1/M3: a confused expression is feedback that calls for clarification and a check. Louder jargon does not address meaning, skipping abandons the learning goal, and extra terms can increase semantic noise.

questions.question: An oral citation during a speech should include at minimum:
options: The author's institutional affiliation and degree credentials
The source's title, author or publication, and date
The database where the article was found and its access date
All information that would appear in a Works Cited entry
questions.answer: The source's title, author or publication, and date
questions.explanation: Oral citations establish credibility by identifying the source to the audience—at minimum including who, where published, and when.

questions.question: A chronological speech organizational pattern is most appropriate when:
options: The topic has three natural, parallel subtopics of equal importance
The audience needs to understand a causal relationship between events
The speech explains a process or historical development in time order
The speaker is comparing two opposing positions on an issue
questions.answer: The speech explains a process or historical development in time order
questions.explanation: Chronological organization arranges content by time sequence—ideal for how-to processes, historical narratives, or biographical accounts.

questions.question: Audience analysis should be conducted before writing a speech because it:
options: Allows the speaker to select the most impressive vocabulary to use
Helps the speaker adapt topic, language, examples, and appeals to maximize relevance and impact
Determines the correct citation format to use for source materials
Establishes the speaker's credibility with the audience before the speech begins
questions.answer: Helps the speaker adapt topic, language, examples, and appeals to maximize relevance and impact
questions.explanation: Audience analysis informs every speech decision—from topic selection to language choice to appeal strategy—ensuring the message resonates with the specific audience.
